entry.title: JPL x Blue Origin | NXT in Space: Episode 6

media:group.media:title: JPL x Blue Origin | NXT in Space: Episode 6
media:group.media:description:
Getting to the Moon is one challenge. Building a lasting presence there is another. What will it take to make that vision a reality – and how can JPL and industry help build that future?
In the final NXT in Space event of 2026, Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp and JPL Director Dave Gallagher explore the infrastructure, technologies, and partnerships needed to advance space exploration over the next decade and beyond. Together, they discuss lunar exploration, planetary protection, and where scientific opportunity meets commercial ambition.
About the guests: Dave Limp joined Blue Origin as CEO in December 2023. Previously, he was Senior VP of Amazon Devices and Services, leading the development of Alexa, Echo, Kindle, and other major initiatives. Limp began his career at Apple, rising to Director of the PowerBook division. He later served as Chief Strategy Officer at both Liberate Technologies and Palm and as a Venture Partner at Azure Capital. He currently sits on the Prometheus AI board and chairs Blue Origin’s Club for the Future, promoting STEAM careers.
Dave Gallagher is the 11th Director of JPL, appointed in 2025 after serving as Associate Director for Strategic Integration. Over the course of his JPL career, Dave has held senior roles within Astronomy, Physics, and Space Technology and the Advanced Optical Systems Program Office. He also served in leadership positions on major NASA missions, including the team responsible for correcting the optical flaw in the Hubble Space Telescope, the Spitzer Space Telescope, and other flagship astrophysics and space technology programs.
NXT in Space is a series from NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory that brings together industry leaders, creatives, and futurists to explore how collaboration can accelerate innovation and push the boundaries of what’s possible. Watch the series: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLTiv_XWHnOZpzDsI4YDrPgASidbJBQhe7
Credit: JPL-Caltech

entry.title: Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day: How to Participate in NASA’s Global Activation

media:group.media:title: Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day: How to Participate in NASA’s Global Activation
media:group.media:description:
NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching a historic milestone, reaching a distance of one light-day from Earth. To celebrate this once-in-human-history moment, join our “Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day” activation, and help us create a wave of golden light around the globe.
After sunset on Nov. 17, 2026, use your smartphone, tablet, or flashlight to signal Voyager’s call sign, V-G-R, in Morse code toward the sky.
Record your celebration and share it with @NASA on social media.
Your light can be tiny, but the moment is huge.
A simple act. A shared moment. A celebration of humanity’s farthest reach.
For more information on the activation, visit: https://go.nasa.gov/shinebright
Learn more about NASA’s Voyager mission: https://nasa.gov/voyager
Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

entry.title: How Far Away Is Voyager 1? One Light-Day, Explained

media:group.media:title: How Far Away Is Voyager 1? One Light-Day, Explained
media:group.media:description:
NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching a historic milestone. On November 18, 2026, the spacecraft will reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.
Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, transformed our understanding of the solar system through their exploration of the outer planets. In 2012, Voyager 1 became the first human-made spacecraft to enter interstellar space.
Now more than 16 billion miles from Earth, Voyager 1 continues its journey into the unknown. At this extraordinary distance, a command sent from Earth takes 24 hours to reach the spacecraft, and another 24 hours for a response to return.
Carrying the Golden Record, a message from humanity, NASA’s farthest explorer continues pushing the boundaries of space exploration nearly five decades after launch.
For more information on the milestone, visit: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/voyager-1/voyager-1-what-is-a-light-day/
Learn more about NASA’s Voyager mission: https://nasa.gov/voyager
Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

Voyager 1 will soon cross a new milestone for humanity.
Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 and its twin Voyager 2 explored our solar system like never before.

entry.title: PROMISE: NASA’s Nuclear-Powered Rover for the Moon

media:group.media:title: PROMISE: NASA’s Nuclear-Powered Rover for the Moon
media:group.media:description:
NASA will send a nuclear-powered rover called PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration, depicted in the rendering) to the Moon’s South Pole as a foundational mission in the Moon Base Program. The PROMISE concept was unveiled by NASA in June 2026; the agency announced on Nov. 7, 2026, it was moving ahead with the mission.
The rover will study the lunar surface and subsurface, prospect for resources, and gather data to support the establishment of humanity’s first lunar outpost.
It will be constructed largely from existing hardware — test-bed and flight-spare components — developed for NASA’s ongoing Mars rover missions, Curiosity and Perseverance (whose vehicle system test bed is shown at the opening of this video). NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California manages those Mars missions, and it is also managing PROMISE on behalf of the agency’s Human Spaceflight Mission Directorate.
PROMISE will carry an extensive payload of science instruments and technology demonstrations. With a multi-mission radioisotope thermoelectric generator on board as a constant source of heat and power, PROMISE will be able to operate in the dark over the long lunar nights and in the Moon’s frigid permanently shadowed regions, where water ice is likely to be found.
Learn more at https://www.nasa.gov/moonbase/promise
Caltech in Pasadena, California, manages JPL for NASA.

entry.title: What's Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA

media:group.media:title: What's Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA
media:group.media:description:
Meteor showers, a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter, a Voyager 1 milestone, and a November supermoon.
The Southern Taurids peak around November 5, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12. Both offer occasional bright fireballs, even though only a handful of meteors per hour are expected under ideal conditions.
On November 15 and 16, look southeast before sunrise to see Jupiter and Mars appear just 1.2 degrees apart.
The Leonid meteor shower offers another chance to catch shooting stars before dawn on November 17 and 18, after the Moon sets.
NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft reaches a historic one light-day milestone. Join the Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation on November 17. Learn more at nasa.gov/voyager.
And on November 24, watch a full supermoon rise in the east around sunset, the first of three consecutive supermoons – in November, December, and January.

entry.title: JPL at 90: A Legacy of Exploration, A Future of Discovery

media:group.media:title: JPL at 90: A Legacy of Exploration, A Future of Discovery
media:group.media:description:
For 90 years, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory has pushed the boundaries of what’s possible, transforming bold ideas into extraordinary discoveries.
From a small group of rocket pioneers in 1936 to missions exploring Earth, Mars, the outer planets, and beyond, JPL has helped shape humanity’s understanding of the universe.
The people, innovations, and discoveries that have defined JPL’s first 90 years come to life through historic footage, iconic mission moments, and the voices of generations of explorers.
As JPL marks this milestone, we look ahead to the next 90 years of exploration, sharing hopes for the discoveries still to come – and what it will take to keep daring mighty things.
Learn more about NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory: https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/
Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

media:group.media:title: JPL x Firefly Aerospace | NXT in Space: Episode 5
media:group.media:description:
As commercial space companies take on a growing role in exploring the Moon and beyond, what new possibilities does that open up for JPL – and for the future of space exploration?
In this episode of JPL’s NXT in Space speaker series, Firefly Aerospace CEO Jason Kim and JPL Director Dave Gallagher discuss ongoing collaborations on the MoonFall and SkyFall projects and the future of robotic missions that will eventually pave the way for human explorers.
About the guests:
Jason Kim serves as the Chief Executive Officer at Firefly Aerospace. Jason has 25 years of experience in executive management of satellites, rockets, ground systems, and autonomous systems, and has supported hundreds of missions for national security, NASA, and commercial customers. Prior to joining Firefly, Jason served in leadership roles at Millennium Space Systems, Raytheon Intelligence & Space, Northrop Grumman Aerospace Systems, and the U.S. Air Force. His work helps drive critical partnerships with NASA and JPL and supports ambitious endeavors from the Blue Ghost lunar mission to the development of critical hardware for deep-space and lunar infrastructure.
Dave Gallagher is the 11th Director of JPL, appointed in 2025 after serving as Associate Director for Strategic Integration. Over the course of his JPL career, Dave held senior roles within Astronomy, Physics, and Space Technology and the Advanced Optical Systems Program Office. He also served in leadership positions on major NASA missions, including the team responsible for correcting the optical flaw in the Hubble Space Telescope, the Spitzer Space Telescope, and other flagship astrophysics and space technology programs.

entry.title: Welcome to Our Universe: Explore JPL 2026

media:group.media:title: Welcome to Our Universe: Explore JPL 2026
media:group.media:description:
Explore JPL 2026 invited the public for an up-close look at the science, engineering, and technology driving NASA's exploration of the solar system and beyond.
As the Jet Propulsion Laboratory celebrates 90 years of discovery and innovation, guests explored our historic achievements, active space missions, and cutting-edge technologies through exhibits highlighting Missions That Changed the World, Moon to Mars, Missions In Flight, and Makerspace. The event also showcased the partnerships and operations that support NASA's missions.
Visitors stepped inside iconic facilities, including JPL's Space Flight Operations Facility, Spacecraft Assembly Facility, and Microdevices Laboratory. They explored full-scale models of NASA's Perseverance Mars rover, Voyager, and Galileo spacecraft, met scientists and engineers working on NASA's missions, and had the opportunity to meet NASA astronaut Alvin Drew. Visitors also attended Caltech LIVE, a series of science talks featuring Caltech researchers.
This special two-day event celebrated JPL’s 90 years of exploration and invited the next generation of scientists, engineers, and explorers to imagine what comes next. Enjoy the highlights!
Learn more: https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/explore-jpl/
Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/
